name: Daria Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Daria, thanks for your time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything here is confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a troubleshooter at the Hollins Cross depot, which covers a market town and about thirty villages. When a fuse blows on a pole transformer or someone's house goes dark, I'm the first one out in the van to find the fault and get them back on. I like being on my own, sorting it, and getting the thank-you wave from the porch. What wears me out is the on-call weeks, when the phone can go any time of night.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my boyfriend Kostas in a rented terrace on Mill Lane. He fixes tyres at the place on the bypass. Neither of us earns much, and we've got maybe three weeks of savings. My dad lives ten minutes away, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, fewer things to worry about. I've never used any of it and don't plan to. I wouldn't post anything, I don't do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my worry isn't AI at all. The company's talking about closing our depot at Hollins Cross and running everything from the city depot, fifty kilometres away. That would mean an hour each way, more fuel, and probably losing on-call because they'd pick people closer in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and wait to see what they decide about the depot. I'd start putting a bit aside in case I need a second car or a change of shifts. I'm not jumping before they jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but nothing to do with computers. The depot's the thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would losing on-call mean for your money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About three hundred a month. That's our food money basically. We'd be living on Kostas's wage plus my basic, and that doesn't cover the rent and the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you thought about what you'd do if the depot closes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, I don't like thinking about it till it happens. My dad says I could work at his mate's electrical shop, but that's half the pay.

say: I'd say **good**, fewer things to worry about.
I've never used AI and **don't plan to**, so I'd keep quiet online.
think: My real worry is the company **closing Hollins Cross** depot.
Moving to the city depot could cost me **on-call** pay, about three hundred a month.
do: Keep my **head down** until they decide about the depot.
Put a bit aside for a **second car** or shift change.
S0.quote: My worry isn't AI at all. The company's talking about closing our depot at Hollins Cross and running everything from the city depot, fifty kilometres away.
fieldNote: The **depot closure** is a real threat to her income, separate from AI.
She **waits** rather than plans, true to her resistant streak.
Her **dad** is her safety net, but his offer pays half.

steps.text: Wait for the company's decision on the Hollins Cross depot
Put aside a little each month for a second car

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office lot who'll feel it first. I'd say it in the canteen, not online. Out on the van there's nothing a computer can do except send me the address.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me, because the company would use it as another excuse to centralise. If the computer plans the jobs and routes the vans from the city, they don't need a depot out here at all. And I'd be the one driving an hour each way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wait and see, honestly, but save harder. I'd cut the takeaway on Fridays and the phone upgrade. If they made me use a tablet with some AI thing, I'd use it, but grudgingly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It feels like the computer gives them the excuse they've been after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the depot closed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The managers in the city who've never been out on a call. Not the computer, the people who use it to cut corners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look at other jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There aren't any round here that pay the same. Maybe the water company, but they're cutting too. So I'd stay and hope.

say: The **office lot** will feel it first, not people on the van.
I'd say that in the **canteen**, not online.
think: AI routing gives the company an **excuse to centralise** and close our depot.
I'd end up **driving an hour** each way to the city.
do: **Wait and see** what the company does with the depot.
Cut the **Friday takeaway** and the phone upgrade to save harder.
Use a **tablet** only if the company makes me.
feel: **Anxious**, because the computer hands managers the **excuse** they wanted.
S1.quote: If the computer plans the jobs and routes the vans from the city, they don't need a depot out here at all.
fieldNote: She links AI to the **depot threat**, which makes it personal.
She blames **managers**, not the technology, a pragmatic view.
**Few local jobs** leave her with no real alternative.

steps.text: Wait for the depot decision before looking elsewhere
Drop the Friday takeaway and the phone upgrade

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disaster and someone should slow it down. I'd sign whatever petition is going round. I wouldn't march, but I'd vote for whoever promised to protect jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means the depot's gone almost straight away, because the planning and dispatch would all be AI by 2028. Then by 2031 there's a robot that can climb and fix a transformer. I'd be 32 with no other skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my dad if we could move in with him to save rent. I'd ask about his mate's electrical shop, half pay or not. And I'd stop all spending that isn't food, rent or fuel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. The night a pole snapped in front of me on the Grange Road, I just froze for a second. Picturing AGI by 2028 feels like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Kostas say about moving in with your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd hate it. But his tyre job would probably go too, with self-driving vans and robots in the garage. So we'd both need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd learn, even if you don't like computers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd have to. But who'd teach me, and when? I'd be working every hour I could to pay the bills.

say: It's a **disaster** and someone should **slow it down**.
I'd sign petitions and **vote** for whoever protects jobs.
think: The **depot** would close almost at once with AI dispatch by 2028.
By **2031** a robot fixes transformers, and I'd have no other skills.
do: Ask my dad if we can **move in** with him to save rent.
Ask about the job at **his mate's shop**, even at half pay.
feel: **Frightened**, like the night a pole **snapped** in front of her.
S2.quote: The night a pole snapped in front of me on the Grange Road, I just froze for a second. Picturing AGI by 2028 feels like that.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** and has no backup skill.
Her boyfriend's **tyre job** is also exposed, doubling the risk.
She can't see **when** she'd find time to learn anything new.

steps.text: Move in with her dad to stop paying rent
Ask about a job at her dad's friend's electrical shop
Vote for the candidate who promises to protect jobs
Stop all spending except food, rent and fuel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say they should give people proper notice and help. Five years is something, but not if you spend it pretending. I'd say that at the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably still pretend for the first couple of years. That's me. But the dispatch goes in 2031 and the robots come in 2034, so I'd have till I'm 35 to sort something out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, aim for two months. In year two or three I might ask the company about a course, maybe in substation work or something they say robots won't do yet. And I'd keep the depot job as long as it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not frozen. More like a long drive with the fuel light on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd pretend. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's easier. I don't like change, never have. I'd rather wait until there's no choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd tell me to get on with it. My dad was a miner. He saw what happened when the pits shut, and he'd tell me not to wait for the letter.

say: People need **proper notice** and help from the company.
Five years is something, but **not if you pretend**.
think: I'd probably **pretend** for the first couple of years.
With robots in **2034**, I'd have till 35 to sort something out.
do: Ask the company about a **substation course** in year two or three.
Keep the **depot job** as long as it lasts.
feel: **Worried**, like a long drive with the **fuel light** on.
S3.quote: My dad was a miner. He saw what happened when the pits shut, and he'd tell me not to wait for the letter.
fieldNote: She's **honest** that she'd delay, which is rare.
Her dad's **mining past** is a strong voice in her head.
Five years moves her from **alarmed** to anxious, not further.

steps.text: Save toward two months of bills
Ask the company about a substation course in year two
Stay on the depot troubleshooting rota

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is fair warning, and people should use it. I wouldn't say much more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably waste the first five. The thinking stuff goes in 2036 and the robots come about 2039, so I'd be 40. I'd hope the company kept a few of us for the tricky jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, save a bit more each year, and maybe start the substation course around 2030. I'd talk to Kostas about whether we ever buy a house or just keep renting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit guilty, because I know I'd leave it too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help you start earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the company just put me on a course and paid for it. I won't go looking for a course, but I'd turn up if the company paid for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change your plans with Kostas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still not have kids for a while. Not with this hanging over us. That's more about money than robots, honestly.

say: Ten years is **fair warning** and people should use it.
I wouldn't say much more than that **out loud**.
think: I'd probably **waste the first five** years.
At **40** in 2039, I'd hope they keep a few for tricky jobs.
do: Keep working and **save a bit more** each year.
Talk with Kostas about **buying versus renting**.
feel: **Uneasy** and a bit **guilty** about leaving it late.
S4.quote: I won't go looking for a course, but I'd turn up if the company paid for it.
fieldNote: She needs an **outside push** to change, and says so.
Kids are on hold mainly for **money reasons**.
Her thin savings and **few jobs** still make the future shaky.

steps.text: Start a substation course around 2030 if paid
Save a little more from each year's pay rise
Hold off on children until money feels safer

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. No time to do anything. What would help is the company being forced to give notice and pay for training, and keep depots open in small towns.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: About the villages. If a robot's coming from the city, it'll take longer to get out to the villages, and old people wait in the cold. Someone should think about them.

headlineQuote: If a robot's coming from the city, it'll take longer to get out to the villages, and old people wait in the cold.
portrait: Daria is a **27-year-old** troubleshooter at a small-town depot, living with her boyfriend Kostas.
With **three weeks** of savings, she fears the company closing her **depot**.
She avoids technology and admits she'd **wait** until change forces her hand.
Her ex-miner **dad** is her safety net and her conscience.
She's **anxious** in most pictures and **alarmed** when AGI arrives in 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time to do anything.
whatWouldHelp: Firms made to give **notice and training**, and to keep small-town **depots** open.
